questions.qtext:
Let $\Sigma=\{a, b\}$ be an alphabet. Consider two formal languages over $\Sigma$, where $L_{1}$ is known to be a regular language and $L_{2}$ is known to be a nonregular language. Let $L_{\text {new }}$ be a new language constructed by performing an operation on $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$.
Which of the following operations guarantees that $L_{\text {new }}$ will always be a nonregular language, regardless of the specific choices of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$?

options.text: $L_{\text {new }}=\overline{L_{2}}$

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
Here we analyze each option with a counter example

A) take L1= (a+b)* ;L2={a^n b^n,n>=0} make L1UL2 =(a+b)* which is regular

B)take L1={ e } ; L2={a^n b^n,n>=0} make L1nL2={e} which is also regular

C)take L1=(e) ; L2={a^n b^n,n>=0} make L1-L2={ } which is regular

D)we know complement of any nonregular language cannot be regular

so option D is approximate answer for above question
Source solution 2 (score: 0)
$\text{A.}$ $L_{new}$ may not be non-regular
Take $L_1 = (a+b)^*$ and $L_2 = \{ a^n b^n \mid n \ge 0\}$
$L_{new} = L_1 \cup L_2 = (a+b)^* \implies REG$

$\text{B. }$ $L_{new}$ may not be non-regular
Take $L_1 = \phi$ and $L_2 = \{ a^n b^n \mid n \ge 0\}$
$L_{new} = L_1 \cup L_2 = \phi \implies REG$

$\text{C. }$ $L_{new}$ may not be non-regular
Take $L_1 = \phi$ and $L_2 = \{ a^n b^n \mid n \ge 0\}$
$L_{new} = L_1 - L_2 = \phi \implies REG$

$\text{D. }$ $L_{new}$ must be non-regular
Since, if ${L_{new}}$ were regular, then $L_2=\overline{{L_{new}}}$ would also be regular (since regular langauges are closure under complementation), contradicting that $L_2$ is non-regular.

Correct Answer: $D$

questions.qtext:
Let $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ be two regular languages over the same alphabet $\Sigma$. Suppose $M_{1}=\left(S_{1}, \Sigma, \delta_{1}, s_{1}, F_{1}\right)$ and $M_{2}=\left(S_{2}, \Sigma, \delta_{2}, s_{2}, F_{2}\right)$ are Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs) such that $L\left(M_{1}\right)=L_{1}$ and $L\left(M_{2}\right)=L_{2}$.
To prove that the class of regular languages is closed under union, we construct a product DFA $M=\left(S_{1} \times S_{2}, \Sigma, \delta,\left(s_{1}, s_{2}\right), F\right)$ that accepts the language $L_{1} \cup L_{2}$.
Which of the following correctly defines the set of accept states $F$ for the product DFA $M$?

options.text: $F=\left(F_{1} \times S_{2}\right) \cup\left(S_{1} \times F_{2}\right)$
$F=\left(F_{1} \times\left(S_{2} \backslash F_{2}\right)\right) \cup\left(\left(S_{1} \backslash F_{1}\right) \times F_{2}\right)$
$F=\left(S_{1} \times S_{2}\right) \backslash\left(F_{1} \times F_{2}\right)$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

The correct answer is:

$$F = (F_1 \times S_2) \cup (S_1 \times F_2)$$

Why? (The Product Automaton Logic)

The product DFA $M$ tracks the processing of a string through both $M_1$ and $M_2$ simultaneously in parallel. Each state in the product DFA is a pair $(q_a, q_b)$, where $q_a \in S_1$ and $q_b \in S_2$.

Since we want the product machine to accept the union ($L_1 \cup L_2$), it needs to accept a string if either $M_1$ accepts it, or $M_2$ accepts it, or both accept it.

Let's look at what the correct mathematical expression actually means:

  • $F_1 \times S_2$: This means the first machine lands in an accepting state ($q_a \in F_1$), while the second machine can be in any state whatsoever ($q_b \in S_2$).

  • $S_1 \times F_2$: This means the first machine can be in any state whatsoever ($q_a \in S_1$), while the second machine lands in an accepting state ($q_b \in F_2$).

  • $\cup$ (Union): Combines these two conditions. As long as at least one of the machines is in an accepting state when the string ends, the product DFA outputs an Accept.

You can easily decode what the other options represent to cross-verify your answer:

  • $F = F_1 \times F_2$

    • What it means: Both machines must be in an accepting state simultaneously.

    • Language it defines: Intersection ($L_1 \cap L_2$)

  • $F = (F_1 \times (S_2 \setminus F_2)) \cup ((S_1 \setminus F_1) \times F_2)$

    • What it means: Exactly one machine must accept, while the other must reject.

    • Language it defines: Symmetric Difference / XOR ($L_1 \oplus L_2$)

  • $F = (S_1 \times S_2) \setminus (F_1 \times F_2)$

    • What it means: Total possible states minus the states where both accept.

    • Language it defines: NAND ($\overline{L_1 \cap L_2}$)

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Correct Answer: $\boxed{B}$

In the product DFA $M$, each state is of the form $(p,q)$, where $p \in S_1$ and $q \in S_2$. A string $w$ is accepted by the $M$ iff at least one of the component DFAs accepts $w$, since the $L(M)$ is $L_1 \cup L_2$.

Thus, a state $(p,q)$ must be accepting whenever:

  • $p \in F_1$ (i.e., $M_1$ accepts) or

  • $q \in F_2$ (i.e., $M_2$ accepts)

Hence, the set of accepting states is

$$
\boxed{F=(F_1\times S_2)\ \cup\ (S_1\times F_2)}
$$

questions.qtext:
Let $L$ be a regular language. We define a new language $L_{\text {sym }}$ that contains all strings in $L$ whose reversals are also in $L$ :
$$
L_{\mathrm{sym}}=\left\{w \in L \mid w^{R} \in L\right\}
$$
Is the language $L_{\text {sym }}$ guaranteed to be regular ?

options.text: No, because checking if a string matches its reversal requires a stack.
Yes, because $L_{\text {sym }}$ can be written as $L \cup L^{R}$. Since regular languages are closed under reversal and union, $L_{\text {sym }}$ is regular.
No, because regular languages are not closed under the reversal operation unless the language is finite.
Yes, because $L_{\text {sym }}$ can be written as $L \cap L^{R}$. Since regular languages are closed under reversal and intersection, $L_{\text {sym }}$ is regular.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
The above question defines a new language such that it contains both w and w reverse now we need the language to contain both L and L reverse or neither so it means we need intersection of L and L reverse. since it is closed under regular operation we can say that it is regular.



(D) is correct
Source solution 2 (score: 0)
Correct Answer: $\boxed{D}$
$$
L_{\text{sym}}=\{w\in L \mid w^R\in L\}
=\{w\mid w\in L \text{ and } w\in L^R\}
= L\cap L^R
$$
Since $L$ is regular, $L^R$ is also regular (closure under reversal). Moreover, regular languages are closed under intersection. Therefore, $L_{\text{sym}}=L\cap L^R$ is regular.

questions.qtext:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. Let $L_{1}, L_{2} \subseteq \Sigma^{*}$ be two languages such that $L_{1}$ is a regular language and $L_{2}$ is not a regular language. In addition, we are given the following conditions:

  • $L_{2} \nsubseteq L_{1}$
  • $L_{1} \nsubseteq L_{2}$
  • $L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ is an infinite set.

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.text: $L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ can be a regular language.
$L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ can be a non-regular language.
$L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ must be a non-regular language.
$L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ must be a regular language.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Option A: L1 ∩ L2 can be regular

L1 is regular. So let L1 = {a*}

L2 is non regular. So let L2 = { aⁿ bⁿ | n ≥ 1 } U {a*} It is a non regular as the first part of language is non-regular.

L1 ∩ L2 = {a*} It is infinite and a regular language.

✅ Option A is True

Option B: L1 ∩ L2 can be non-regular

Let L1 = Σ* It is a regular language.

Let L2 = { aⁿ bⁿ | n ≥ 0 } It is a non-regular language.

L1 ∩ L2 = { aⁿ bⁿ | n ≥ 0 } It is infinite and a non-regular language.

✅ Option B is True

Option C: L1 ∩ L2 must be a non-regular language

It is false. Valid example is given for Option A

❌ Option C is False

Option D: L1 ∩ L2 must be a regular language

It is false. Valid example is given for Option B

❌ Option D is False

Therefore, the false statements are C and D.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

$\boxed{\textbf{C and D}}$

  1. True. $L_1 \cap L_2$ can be regular.

    Eg: Let $L_1=L(a^*)$ and $L_2=\{a^n b^n\mid n\ge1\}\cup \{a^n \mid n\ge5\}$. Then $L_1\cap L_2=\{a^n \mid n\ge5\}$, which is regular.

  2. True. $L_1 \cap L_2$ can be non-regular.

    Eg: Let $L_1= L(a^* b^*) $ and $L_2=\{a^n b^n \mid n\ge1\}\cup\{b^n a^m\mid n \ge 1\}$. Then $L_1\cap L_2=\{a^n b^n\mid n\ge1\}$, which is non-regular.

  3. False. Since $L_1 \cap L_2$ can be regular (Option A), it is not necessary that it is non-regular.

  4. False. Since $L_1 \cap L_2$ can be non-regular (Option B), it is not necessary that it is regular.

questions.qtext:
Let $A$ be a finite automaton that accepts a regular language $L$. We want to build a new automaton $\overline{A}$ that accepts the reversed language $L^{R}$ (the language containing all strings of $L$ written backward).
To do this, we reverse the direction of all arrows in the transition diagram of $A$. What must we do with the start and accepting states to complete the construction of $\overline{A}$?

options.text: In $\overline{A}$, create a new start state with $\varepsilon$-transitions to all accepting states of $A$, and keep the accepting states of $A$ as accepting while also making the start state of $A$ an accepting state of $\overline{A}$.
Keep the start state of $A$ as the start state of $\overline{A}$, and make all accepting states of $A$ the new accepting states of $\overline{A}$.

Create a single new start state that connects to all of $\text{A's}$ accepting states using $\varepsilon$-transitions, and make the original start state of $A$ the only accepting state of $\overline{A}$.
Make the start state of $A$ the only accepting state of $\overline{A}$, and turn all accepting states of $A$ into multiple start states of $\overline{A}$.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Option c is correct.

Why This Works

When you reverse a language, you need to reverse everything about the automaton — not just the arrows, but also the roles of the start and accepting states.

Here's the intuition: a string w=a1a2⋯anw = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n w=a1​a2​⋯an​ is accepted by AA A if there's a path from the start state to some accepting state. The reversed string wR=an⋯a2a1w^R = a_n \cdots a_2 a_1 wR=an​⋯a2​a1​ should be accepted by A′A' A′ if that same path can be traversed backwards — meaning we now start from the old accepting state(s) and need to reach the old start state.

So the role-swap is:

In AA AIn A′A' A′
Start stateAccepting state
Accepting statesStart state(s)
The Problem That Option 3 Solves

After reversing all arrows, there may be multiple old accepting states that should each serve as a starting point. But a standard DFA requires exactly one start state. The clean solution is:

  1. Introduce a new start state q0′q_0' q0′​
  2. Add ε\varepsilon ε-transitions from q0′q_0' q0′​ to every accepting state of AA A
  3. Make the original start state of AA A the sole accepting state of A′A' A′

This correctly models "start anywhere a valid path used to end" without requiring the reversal automaton to be a DFA — it produces an NFA with ε\varepsilon ε-transitions (an ε\varepsilon ε-NFA), which can then be converted to a DFA if needed. The existence of this construction is actually one of the standard proofs that the class of regular languages is closed under reversal.

Why the Others Fail
OptionProblem
1Keeps the same start and accepting states — this just builds the same automaton with reversed arrows, which doesn't correctly trace reversed paths
2The direction is right (swap start ↔ accept), but having "multiple independent start states" is not valid in standard automata; you need the ε\varepsilon ε-NFA trick to unify them
4Merging all accepting states destroys the automaton's structure and swapping all state roles has no theoretical justification
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option $C$ is correct

questions.qtext:
For any language $A$, we define the prefix language $\operatorname{PREFIX}(A)$ as the set of all strings $w$ that form a string in $A$ when some suffix string $x$ is appended to them:
$$
\operatorname{PREFIX}(A)=\left\{w \mid \exists x \in \Sigma^{*} \text { such that } w x \in A\right\}
$$
Let $M=\left(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_{0}, F\right)$ be a DFA that recognizes the regular language $A$. We want to construct a new finite automaton $M^{\prime}=\left(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_{0}, F^{\prime}\right)$ that precisely recognizes $\operatorname{PREFIX}(A)$.
To achieve this without changing the states, alphabet, transition function, or start state of $M$, how should the new set of accepting states $F^{\prime}$ be defined?

options.text: $F^{\prime}=\{q \in Q \mid q \notin F\}$
$F^{\prime}=\left\{q \in Q \mid\right.$ there is a path from $q_{0}$ to $\left.q\right\}$
$F^{\prime}=\{q \in Q \mid$ there is a path from $q$ to some state in $F\}$
$F^{\prime}=\{q \in F \mid \delta(q, \sigma) \in F$ for all $\sigma \in \Sigma\}$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

  • $F' = \{q \in Q \mid q \notin F\}$

    • What it means: Swapping accepting and non-accepting states.

    • What it actually constructs: The Complement language ($\overline{A}$), not the prefix.

  • $F' = \{q \in Q \mid \text{there is a path from } q_0 \text{ to } q\}$

    • What it means: Every reachable state accepts.

    • What it actually constructs: A machine that blindly accepts any string that doesn't crash the DFA, which for a complete DFA is just $\Sigma^*$.

  • $F' = \{q \in F \mid \delta(q, \sigma) \in F \text{ for all } \sigma \in \Sigma\}$

    • What it means: Only looks at states that are already final and can never leave $F$. This restricts the language heavily rather than expanding it to prefixes.

  • Meaning of others is done now for the answer :

Imagine you are tracing a string $w$ in the original DFA $M$, and you end up at a state $q$ (so, $\delta^*(q_0, w) = q$).

  1. If there is a path from $q$ to some state in $F$: It means there exists some sequence of characters $x$ that can take you from $q$ to a final state ($\delta^*(q, x) \in F$). Therefore, the combined string $wx$ is accepted by $M$ (meaning $wx \in A$). This makes $w$ a valid prefix, so $q$ must be an accepting state in our new machine $M'$.

  2. If there is NO path from $q$ to any state in $F$: It means you have hit a "dead end" or a trap state. No matter what characters $x$ come next, you can never reach a final state. Therefore, no string starting with $w$ can ever be in $A$, so $q$ should reject.

By making every state $q$ accepting if it can eventually find a path to the original target $F$, the machine $M'$ will immediately accept the string the moment it knows a valid path to the future exists

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option $C$ is correct.
